sources.title: Presidential biography: birth, provincial administration and defence ministry
sources.findings: Read the government biography birth paragraph and ministerial/provincial section: 5 March 1954, Lobito, Benguela; Moxico commissioner in 1983; Benguela 1986–1989; defence minister from 2014 until the 2017 campaign. Its header labels an election date of 24 August 2017, conflicting with contemporaneous Xinhua reporting of the 23 August general election. Do not adopt that header as either the polling or inauguration date. No birth certificate or complete presidential personnel decrees were inspected.

sources.publisher: Angolan Ministry of Foreign Affairs / Embassy in Japan
sources.title: 2020 official biography: Soviet education and parliamentary and ministerial service
sources.findings: Read the foreign-ministry biography published by the Angolan embassy in Japan on 24 August 2020. It states Soviet military training in 1978–1982, heavy-artillery specialisation and a master’s degree in historical sciences there, without identifying the specific award institution/date. It gives first vice-president of the National Assembly in 2003–2014, defence appointment in 2014 and earlier provincial posts. The 2020 publication date is not a new appointment. Do not turn a master’s into a doctorate, guess the university, or rely on its dated present-tense roles to establish 2026 incumbency.

sources.title: 26 September 2017: Lourenço sworn in after the 23 August general election
sources.findings: Read the contemporaneous Xinhua 26 September 2017 report. It confirms the completed inauguration, succession to José Eduardo dos Santos and the 23 August general election. The predecessor’s long presidential tenure is separate from his continuing party leadership. The article’s remarks about unanimous national support are attributed ceremonial rhetoric and are not treated as public-opinion findings. No event video or photograph pixels were inspected.

sources.title: 2018 MPLA leadership election and anti-corruption commitments
sources.findings: Read RTP’s Lusa account of the MPLA leadership election, its party congress procedure, presidency since 26 September 2017, and the new party leader’s anti-corruption commitments. Promises to combat nepotism and impunity are not proof of eradication. It reports 98.58 percent, while Reuters reports 98.59 percent; the public dossier omits that minor conflicting percentage rather than silently choosing one. Party-election commission claims of a fair internal vote are not independent election certification.

sources.title: 8 September 2018: Lourenço becomes ruling-party leader after separate presidential succession
sources.findings: Read Reuters’s report carried by Euronews, dated 8 September 2018. It distinguishes the 2017 national presidency from the 2018 party succession and records an unopposed internal leadership election. Discussion of prospective cabinet changes and economic diversification is not evidence that all reforms succeeded. Historic accusations or suspect status concerning dos Santos family members are not imported as current criminal verdicts, and the old currency/IMF figures are not used as 2026 economic indicators.

sources.title: S/2022/896, paragraphs 2–3: Angola election, challenges and 15 September inauguration
sources.findings: Read the Angola subsection and relevant context in UN Secretary-General report S/2022/896 dated 1 December 2022, paragraphs 2–3. It gives polling on 24 August, announced MPLA vote share of 51.17 percent on 29 August, opposition complaints, the Constitutional Court’s 8 September finality ruling, and the 15 September presidential/vice-presidential inauguration. It also records observer concerns about electoral administration and media coverage. Do not conflate a court’s confirmation of results with absence of electoral criticism, polling with inauguration, or party vote share with a separate personal presidential ballot. The whole regional report and original election judgments were not audited.

sources.title: 15 February 2025: Lourenço takes over rotating AU chairmanship
sources.findings: Read ENA’s short contemporaneous 15 February 2025 report, explicitly stating the AU chairmanship was assumed that day at the opening of the 38th summit. It supersedes a later March publication/profile date as evidence for the beginning of this one-year rotating office. This office is separate from the African Union Commission chairperson and from an AU peace-champion designation.

sources.title: 5 April 2025 Assembly Bureau meeting endorses proposed replacement mediator
sources.findings: Read the AU’s 5 April 2025 Assembly Bureau meeting record. Lourenço chaired the virtual meeting, explained his intended withdrawal from DRC–Rwanda mediation, proposed Faure Gnassingbé and obtained Bureau endorsement. The record expressly describes formal Assembly concurrence as still required; 5 April endorsement alone is not the final appointment. Do not carry the mediation office forward indefinitely or claim the conflict ended. The Commission chair attending the meeting is a different official and institutional office.

sources.title: 16 April 2025: newly appointed AU mediator Gnassingbé meets Lourenço in Luanda
sources.findings: Read the Togolese presidency’s 16 April 2025 report of Gnassingbé’s actual Luanda visit and talks with Lourenço as newly appointed AU mediator. It dates formal designation to 12 April, distinct from the 5 April proposal and subsequent news publication dates. The public chronology uses April without unnecessary day-level precision for the handover. The official account’s praise of diplomatic achievements and hopes for an effective ceasefire are not independent proof that peace was achieved or all armed groups complied.

sources.title: 14 February 2026: Ndayishimiye succeeds Lourenço as rotating AU chair
sources.findings: Read the African Union’s 14 February 2026 summit release confirming that Évariste Ndayishimiye succeeded Lourenço in the rotating chairmanship. The AU’s current roster separately lists Burundi for February 2026–February 2027 and Angola for February 2025–February 2026. The public role no longer calls Lourenço current AU chair. Neither the Assembly chair nor Angola’s rapporteur position is equivalent to chair of the AU Commission.

sources.title: World Report 2026, Angola: events of 2025
sources.findings: Read the heading and selected assembly, press-freedom and fair-trial sections of Human Rights Watch’s World Report 2026 Angola chapter. The page explicitly covers events of 2025. Its accounts of protest policing, arbitrary arrests and media restrictions are attributed to the organisation, not described as 2026 events or judicial findings of Lourenço’s personal guilt. It also reports the police announcement of an investigation and their denial of shoot-to-kill orders. No current outcome of each investigation or individual criminal case was verified; disputed casualty totals and Cabinda allegations are not imported into the public profile.

sources.title: 14 November 2026 report: party leadership contest and unresolved 2027 national candidacy
sources.findings: Read DW Africa/Lusa’s report published on 14 November 2026, including quoted remarks made at an industrial-technology-centre inauguration in Luanda. It identifies him as current president and MPLA leader and distinguishes his sole admitted party-leadership candidacy from the as-yet-unannounced candidate for the 2027 national election. The date in the timeline is the report publication date; the exact event/interview date was not independently established. The report discusses a planned December congress, not a completed re-election. Its two-term-limit context is consistent with the constitutional text, without projecting unverified future rule changes or naming a successor.

sources.title: 7 November 2026 publication on 5 November approval of party-leadership candidacy
sources.findings: Read the MPLA’s official report: webpage publication 7 November 2026, dateline 6 November, and Central Committee meeting/approval on Thursday 5 November. It records approval of Lourenço’s candidacy for party president and his chairing of the preceding Political Bureau meeting. Approval is not a completed leadership election and is not nomination for the 2027 national presidency. The party’s praise of its leadership is not independent validation of democratic or economic outcomes.

sources.title: Angola 2010 Constitution, Articles 109 and 113: national-list election and presidential terms
sources.findings: Read the Constitute Project’s English rendering of the 2010 Constitution, selected Articles 106, 108–114. Article 109 ties presidential election to the first name on the national list of the party or coalition with most votes, while Article 106 describes universal direct suffrage. Therefore the accurate distinction is absence of a separate presidential ballot, not a claim that voters are entirely excluded or that parliament directly elects the president. Article 113 states a five-year term and a two-term limit. This is a historical constitutional edition, not a full audit of all subsequent amendments; contemporary DW reporting supplies current electoral context.
